title: A Rib of the Earth
story:
James sat at the edge of the rocky depression, his fingers brushing the cold, exposed ridge of the buried spine. In the Great Canopy, everything changed. Leaves withered, bark softened, and damp soil swallowed the fallen. But this ridge did not yield. It did not warm under his touch, nor did it crumble under his fingernails. It remained stubborn, silent, and entirely indifferent to the sun.

He had never known a vine that did not grow. He had never known a branch that did not bend. He had never known a bone that did not decay. Yet here was a rib of the earth itself, cold and grey, refusing to belong to the forest he knew. Near its base, half-hidden in the coarse gravel, lay a smaller piece that had come free—a heavy, hollow circle of the same grey material, polished smooth by years of wind and dust. James picked it up, surprised by its weight. It fit comfortably in his palm, solid and strangely grounding.

With his new treasure clutched tight, James stepped out of the depression and made his way down to the very lip of the vast grey-green valley, a place the elders of the Canopy had sometimes warned of as the Whispering Flats. The air here was thinner, carrying that sharp metallic scent he had chased from the hillside. As he paused to look out over the shimmering expanse, a new sound drifted to him on the breeze. It was not the sigh of the wind, nor the cry of a mountain bird. It was a rhythmic, repeating clack-clack-clack, mechanical and precise, echoing from somewhere far beyond the horizon where the thin wisp of smoke had first risen.

James held the heavy ring up to his ear, as if it might be a shell echoing the distant noise. The sound had already faded, leaving only the quiet rush of the wind through the low, dusty shrubs. He looked down at the strange ring in his hand, then back toward the vast, empty flats. Tonight, the horizon felt a little closer, and a little less silent.
location: the edge of the Whispering Flats
